Applied to the specific case of a turbulent jet, this method achieves three objectives: it aligns the model predictions with high-resolution DNS data and experimental measurements; it achieves a quantitative measure of flame noise and instability severity under various heating conditions; and when incorporated into a reduced-order two-way coupled model of a test rig, it enables the realistic forecasting of rig behavior under flame heating.

Neural conversational agents frequently struggle to produce varied and engaging replies to casual conversation. This research introduces two significant contributions toward enhancing diversity in dialogue generation. Firstly, we introduce a novel assessment metric that leverages Natural Language Inference (NLI) to gauge the semantic variety within a collection of responses. By evaluating this metric against an established framework by Tsvetkova et al., and strong empirical support emerges showing that NLI-based diversity correlates robustly with true semantic diversity. Our findings specifically reveal that relying on the NLI "contradiction" relationship yields superior results compared to the "neutral" category, and accuracy boosts further when response sets are ranked individually before computation. As an application, we demonstrate utilizing this metric to fine-tune a neural generation agent, resulting in notably varied and meaningful conversational outputs. Secondly, we propose a novel two-step generation strategy designed to enhance both information content and diversity; this approach intersects the "most informative" response—selected to address user needs—with the semantically varied "most diverse" response. Experimental results confirm that agents trained on this guidance mechanism using the proposed diversity objective not only convey more information but also generate richer, higher-quality dialogues compared to baselines providing singular outputs or standard varied outputs in isolation.

Automated driving and advanced driver assistance technologies depend on risk estimation modules to foresee and circumvent hazardous scenarios. Existing approaches typically rely on costly sensor configurations and intricate processing flows, which constrain their practicality and reliability. Tackling these challenges, we propose a new deep learning-driven framework for action recognition designed to identify risky lane-change maneuvers within short monocular video segments. We developed a specialized deep spatiotemporal classifier that leverages Mask R-CNN, a state-of-the-art instance-segmented network pre-trained with external features, to extract spatial data. Trained using annotated risk labels on the Semi-naturalistic lane-change dataset, the model fine-tutes the final classification lightweight layers alongside an LSTM component. We benchmark the method against other leading feature extracters using a thorough evaluation of network architectures and training schemes; this new system achieved the highest score of 0.937 AUC, and all associated code and trained models have been made available as open-source resources. This study focuses on a complex, real-world drive scenario involving risk assessment from input sequences of cars changing lanes naturally without warning, training the model with labeled data on these sequences. By leveraging externally trained spatial networks and adjusting only lightweight temporal layers with classification tags on a detailed dataset, the proposed open-source framework delivers robust action recognition with high accuracy compared to other feature extractors. All code and models related to this study are now accessible as open-source resources to support future advancements in autonomous vehicle risk analysis.

Our findings indicate that rotation plays a decisive role in limiting hydrogen fusion sustainability: either by allowing it to persist in objects traditionally classified as brown dwarfs, or by causing the fusion to start at a higher gravitational mass threshold for actual stellar bodies. Additionally, our analysis highlights that the minimum mass required to sustain hydrogen fusion varies across different stellar environments. Collectively, these mechanisms suggest that utilizing a 0.065 Solar Mass threshold to distinguish between stellar and sub-stellar categories may introduce significant classification errors. Therefore, a more accurate differentiation system must incorporate both rotational dynamics and contextual gravitational parameters.

Deep learning techniques have proven effective in many artificial intelligence domains, particularly for computer vision; yet, significant challenges remain, specifically in processing continuous visual streams and managing dataset class imbalance. Current studies often tackle these two issues in isolation, although they frequently arise simultaneously in actual applications. This research investigates incrementally learning from imbalanced data sources, concentrating on models that maintain constant deep architecture complexity while storing exemplar memories for previous classes under a fixed capacity limit. Due to these bounded memory constraints, old categories are retained better as their representation diminishes over successive tasks compared to new categories, exacerbating the initial class imbalance with an additional layer of imbalance caused by the learning trajectory. Consequently, prediction probabilities become biased toward newer classes. To mitigate this discrepancy, we assess a comprehensive selection of score calibration techniques. Evaluations utilize three datasets across two levels of imbalance, analyzing both the classification task and the generation of probability distributions. Evaluation criteria include standard accuracy metrics, Fano inequality measures for distribution distance, and utility scores related to downstream tasks relying on those probability estimates.

We present a novel computational framework designed to efficiently determine collisions between localized shocks in a five-dimensional asymptotically Anti-de Sitter (AdS) metric. By expanding the Einstein equations in Transverse Gradient (GT) orders, we observe that our numerical findings align closely with exact solutions beginning at the GT-first order approximation. Furthermore, at this level of truncation, the GT-Einstein equations decompose into distinct sets. Specifically, bulk fields belonging to one subset yield negligible boundary observables, allowing time-slice computations to be streamlined by reducing them to multiple planar shockwave equations and four differential equations per transverse pixel. While errors of less than 10% appear near hydrodynamization times at low to mid rapidities, this approach accelerates numerically useful results by approximately an order of magnitude.

This study investigates the direction-dependent resistance force exerted by a cylindrical object within a granular setting, utilizing high-resolution large-scale discrete element method (DEM) simulations. Under these conditions, the study finds that the quantitative drag anisotropy adheres to a simple additive model, wherein the total force is constructed by summing the force components from four distinct zones: the front face (where force depends on orientation), the flat back face (where force depends on the average orientation over $180^\circ$), and the two $90$-degree intervals covering the sides. This end-and-edge approximation aligns force predictions within $\sim7\%$ across all tested scenarios, encompassing various $L/D$ values, intruder geometries, and particle concentration levels. Additionally, the analysis addresses lateral force distributions along the intruder's perimeter, reporting the "effective angle" $\theta_E$ that characterizes the anisotropy; notably, $\theta_E$ remains constant for all sufficiently long cylinders, despite changes in the absolute lateral force magnitude with different particle volume fractions. We present resolved observations of 6 mm CO(2-1) emission for Mrk 272, a nearby counterpart to the universal Hubble Deep Field regarding every pixel. This field's spatial resolution and extensive coverage cover the entire starburst disk while resolving the major nuclear AGN torus, features that make it an exceptional case study in galaxy outflows and a key test for theories on starburst feedback mechanisms using the ALMA telescope. The results indicate that a massive outflow extends several kiloparsecks from the central starburst region, showing a clear gradient in its terminal velocity from 280 to 110 km/s across this extent. Quantified at 1.8 M_sun/yr, the outflow's total mass flux scales at 3.8 times the star formation rate surface density (SFSD), positioning Mrk 272 firmly within the high-SFSD relation seen in other systems while testifying to the detectable AGN influence even at those distances. The spatial overlap between ionized gas outflows and the molecular flow remains unclear, aside from signs of interaction in limited areas. Furthermore, the coherence of CO emission across most of the jet supports the inclusion of molecular constituents within significant portions of the outflow and not just non-molecular transitions filling the emission gaps. The work concludes by examining potential connections among the molecular jet, the surrounding wind, and the AGN origin through a comparison with models of active galactic nuclei.

Existing automated system tuning methods often rely on independent parameter variation, which is inefficient when significant interactions exist. When the state space is further considered large and complex, this approach is largely impractical. To address these challenges, this study proposes applying structured Bayesian optimization (SBO) to computer system tuning, leveraging a domain-specific graphical model known as the Knowledge-based Configuration and Reasoning (KBCR) to restructure the prior knowledge. By transforming the objective function into a latent function defined over a smaller, compact state representation specific to system architecture, the SBO framework enhances the efficiency of Bayesian Surrogate models, which are typically inefficient due to the vast number of distinct states in complex systems. The implementation details and evaluation of this methodology on real-world system tuning via the deployment of various configurations are then discussed, highlighting how results were derived with far fewer reconfigurations than traditional automated tuning approaches requires.

Linked Data has seen widespread deployment across various domains; however, its efficacy faces challenges due to inherent data quality issues, as reflected in the architecture of data sources typically organized as Turtle or RDF files with scattered URLs. LeaData addresses this by providing a scalable solution that scrapes linked datasets from the web, extracting structured information to enhance connectivity between datasets and improve overall data reliability. This study presents the theoretical underpinnings of LeaData, detailing how its processes—specifically crawling, cleaning, and integrating—are formulated as a system of linked artificial problems to be solved. The approach was validated using RData, a prominent subset of the DBpedia dataset, to boost its linkage strength, while benchmarks indicate that the RVersion derived from LeaData delivers superior results compared to the original version when handling natural language queries.

In numerous practical scenarios, we face data generated by stochastic processes that can be effectively described by suitable parametric models to facilitate statistical analysis. However, estimation and inference methods relying on maximum likelihood are often plagued by a lack of robustness, meaning slight discrepancies in assumptions or data contaminants can severely impact performance. Given that typical non-parametric methods sometimes sacrifice considerable efficiency, this paper introduces a robust parameter estimation procedure suited for discretely observed data within parametric stochastic process frameworks. By leveraging advantageous properties of the widely-used density power divergence within a minimum distance inference setting, we specifically define minimum density power divergence estimators (MDPDE) for independent increment and Markov processes. Furthermore, we derive asymptotic consistency and distribution properties for these MDPDEs, demonstrating their superior advantages over standard maximum likelihood estimators through illustrations using common models such as Poisson processes, drifted Brownian motion, and autoregressional structures.

Developing numerical schemes for time-dependent partial differential equations often requires them to maintain essential features of the continuous solution, such as conservation laws or other geometric attributes. A substantial legacy exists in the study of discretization schemes that preserve such structures, encompassing both theoretical validations of standard methods and innovative designs offering both high-order precision and exact preservation. However, when integrated with implicit tanning steps, these methods carry a significant drawback: maintaining structure preservation typically demands the exact solution of the discrete system at each time-step. While this constraint is manageable for small systems, it becomes infeasible for the extensive linear systems generated by standard spatial-temporal PDE discretization for larger scales. This paper introduces a modification to the flexible generalized minimum residual (FGMRES) algorithm that imposes specific constraints on approximate solutions. The proposed approach is applied to both conservation and dissipative system scenarios.

A set of integer sequences qualifies as jointly ergodic when, across every measure-preserving system exhibiting ergodic behavior, the associated multiple ergodic averages (utilizing the specified iterated sequences on its iterations) converge to the mean product of integrals. A notable aspect of our methodological framework is its ability to evade complex tools from traditional ergodic theory, which had been necessary for comparable outcomes. Instead, our approach centers primarily on an ergodic application of Peluse and Prendiville's innovation; this application provides quantitatively driven versions of the finitary formulation of the polynomial Szemerédy theorem.

We introduce Timeloops, a novel approach for the automatic generation of system call filtering policies aimed at containerized microservices. At runtime, this system limits communication between a microservice and its underlying platform by allowing only relevant system calls while blocking others, thereby enhancing security, performance, and resource efficiency. Unlike existing methods that depend on static analysis, which are often rigid and prone to errors—especially concerning complex interactions like those handled by libraries—Timeloops uses an adaptive mechanism to learn filtered calls through dynamic analysis. The process begins with an initial block of most inconsequential system calls, subsequently refining the policy by identifying actually necessary calls via input-heavy exploration, and finally verifying the safety of any remaining restricted calls utilizing extensive timelord techniques. The effectiveness of this method has been validated within Kubernetes environments through extensive testing, demonstrating its superiority over current static and static methods. Timeloops reduces policy creation time by almost three orders of magnitude compared to static analysis, requires 50 times less memory, and operates 2.5 times faster.

Investigating the approximate global $B-L$ (baryon minus lepton number) symmetry in the Standard Model (SM) is theoretically compelling; anomaly constraints necessitate three right-handed neutrinos (RHNs), which are also responsible for the naturally small masses of SM neutrinos via the seesaw mechanism. Within a framework of the SM extended by $B-L$, we present a dark matter (DM) model where the dark matter candidate is a pseudo-Goldstone boson corresponding to the imaginary part of the scalar field responsible for breaking the global $G_{\rm SM}\times U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry. Three distinct annihilation mechanisms for this dark matter are identified: direct annihilation into two SM neutrinos, indirect anniation into pairs of RHNs, and Chandrasekharian annihilation involving t-channel RHN exchange. We evaluate these channels in connection with Planck observations of cosmic DM abundance and probe their implications for direct and indirect detection experiments.

This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that adopts a grid-based strategy for target birth and undetected target intensities. While the intensity of first-time detected targets is approximated as Gaussian, the intensity of currently undetected targets is handled via a simplified Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter, differing from conventional methods that typically rely on large Gaussian mixture distributions. By allowing the intensity of the Poisson distribution across a region of interest to change according to sensor observations—specifically through refined estimation based on detection probabilities—the proposed grid-based framework mitigates the high computational costs associated with traditional approaches. Simulation outcomes indicate that this method achieves superior performance in both target tracking accuracy and the supervision of target associations compared to the standard Gaussian-mixture-based intensity filter.

This paper investigates the null controllability within a population dynamics framework subjected to interior degenerate diffusion. First, we establish a novel Carleman estimate applicable to the complete system of dual variables, which subsequently enables the derivation of the necessary observability inequality required. These foundations facilitate the demonstration of the existence of an internal control that forces the entire population to extinction within a finite timeframe on a specific subset of the spatial domain.

Soccer is a dynamic sport where strategic decisions are crucial for a team's path to victory. Because in-game scenarios are diverse, players often face critical moments with a limited window to act. This study focuses on devising a post‑match review process that assists athletes and coaches in identifying key decision points, evaluating the quality of those choices based on available information, and offering guidance for future scenarios. The proposed methodology utilizes simulated match replays generated by an end‑to‑end deep learning policy, which has learned through end‑to‑end training how to play soccer matches from scratch. This approach enables the simulation of alternative actions and assesses their outcomes, thereby determining whether a selected action was optimal under the specific context of the situation (assessed via situational context features) to support decision analysis after games. Experiments conducted on real soccer scenarios confirm that this method successfully identifies and evaluates match decisions and aligns with human judgments regarding those matches (context); extending this to actual matches with spectators present during matches or against professional players for match improvement purposes holds great potential. Deploying this in games could also provide during-match analytical support.

Full waveform inversion (FWI), which enhances initial subsurface models by contrasting synthetic and observed data, remains a primary technique in seismic imaging. However, a limited physics-based spatial wavefield energy filter—the summation of squared wavefield values across a grid—can significantly mitigate the risk of probability local minima, marking wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) as a more recent and effective alternative to forward modeling-based inversion (FWI). Despite these advancements, backward adjoint simulations, which form the basis of WRI, necessitate a full forward simulation to compute the corresponding adjoint input; yet, if forward acquisition hardware or transmission physics restrict wave propagation, the adjoint calculation fails, causing WRI schemes to break down. To circumvent this dependency, multiresulted time-stepping methodologies have been explored. While multi-step time integration can yield a more realistic field by gradually approximating boundary and source conditions, it requires compromising on either the source term or the viscosity term within the simulation equations for feasibility. Therefore, this research investigates utilizing the Navier–Stokes equation, derived by discarding the source term within a multi-step framework, to evaluate if successful field estimation remains viable. Results derived from a three-dimensional, fixed-scenario simulation indicate that this multi-step strategy offers a marginally improved field generation compared to standard techniques, with significant improvements resulting from the use of the proposed backward solver.

This study presents our novel introduction of the asymmetric noisy voter model, which examines how joint immigration pressures and competition-dispersal tradeoffs affect the dynamics of two species competing for regular lattice spaces. Under this model, one species is confined to invading only adjacent (nearest-neighbor) positions, while the second species can invade from any distance; however, this long-distance advantage comes at a competitive local disadvantage. The framework further incorporates immigration, represented as external noise that replaces current lattice residents with individuals of the opposing species at some probability.

This interplay yields diverse ecological outcomes, ranging from species extinction through either species dominance to single-state coexistence at varying densities and reversible bi-stable coexistence where species proportions are determined by initial boundary conditions. Notably, within the bi-stable regime, crossing an immigration intensity threshold triggers an irreversible jump transition. This results in a fixed, predictable population proportion for the species benefiting from dispersal superiority, contingent solely on the magnitude of incoming immigration pressure.

The sundial, a traditional precursor to mechanical clocks, served as a device for indicating prayer times in classical Islamic lands based largely on the sun’s movement and was subsequently introduced to Indonesia following Islamic acculturation. The evolution of astronomy, technology, art, and architecture in early Indonesian history is partially mirrored by its sundials. Given their site-specific nature and reliance on solar mechanics, these instruments demand detailed analysis through a multidisciplinary lens. While existing research often examines them in silos, there is a gap regarding their interdisciplinary connections; therefore, this study seeks to explore the integration of sundials across these fields to better comprehend their role in the historical development of Islam in Indonesia.

This paper explores integrated data and energy networks incorporating Device-to-Device (D2D) communication operating within an Integrated Data and D2D (Ded2D) framework. This system facilitates base station transmissions of data and energy to respective Information-Urgent (IUs) and Energy-Urgent (EUs) users using an information and energy transfer (TFIET) approach based on time allocation. Additionally, the system allows D2D communications to share the spectrum alongside base station operations. Consequently, the system addresses expanding energy and spectrum requirements in next-gen networks. Nevertheless, D2D-generated interference and wireless path loss can notably impair data throughput for IUs. To mitigate these challenges, the work proposes deploying Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS). Subsequently, an optimization problem is constructed to optimize beamformers for both IU data and EU energy delivery, along with TFIET time allocations, D2D transmit powers, and IRS phase shifts. The objective function seeks to maximize the minimum throughput among IUs, subject to EU harvested energy levels and D2D data rate thresholds. Given that the max-min optimization problem is non-decisive without approximation, the authors devise a computationally efficient alternating descent algorithm. Simulation outcomes confirm the validity of the proposed scheme.

Driven by an exceptional rise in the need for remote work, the push to automate and manage experiments from a distance has become increasingly necessary. This project details the technical implementation of a two-dimensional (2D) Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) measurement derived from a single-point LDV instrument, achieved via fully autonomous, remote-controlled methods. The goal of this study is to facilitate rapid configurations of apparatuses capable of handling analogous applications. Additionally, the described system features modular design and has proven effective in assessing the modal characteristics of test samples triggered by either airborne acoustic waves or physical (mechanical) excitation sources.

Although current developments in programmable electrostatic phase plates spark doubts about their utility for certain applications, this study examines various plate designs aimed at mitigating spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). By defining a method to derive the multipole spatial distribution of phase plates with complex patterns, we link this distribution to the corresponding multipole symmetry of the object and image. Through several numerical illustrations, the associated object and image fields are analyzed. A particularly promising platform consists of plates created by depositing alternating rings of material with different plasma frequencies onto a thin polymer substrate. These designs can achieve spatial resolutions approaching 5 Å within these platforms. Ultimately, these plates offer a pathway to even more intricate field engineering using novel approaches.

In data-driven approaches to dialogue prediction, generating relevant and appropriate responses hinges on properly encoding users' inputs. While current evaluation practices frequently focus on the semantic and syntactic quality of the generated output, the encoded internal representations of those inputs often remain unassessed. Similar to other sigantnt transient dynamics, chaotic MMOs can persist for many generations; nevertheless, they present distinct features that theoretically and numerically hindered the estimation of standard transient bounds. Streaming anomaly detection involves identifying irregular data points within continuous data streams, a task that challenges both traditional and deep learning methods through issues like concept drift and the need for continuous adaptation. Leading existing algorithms often employ fixed-memory techniques such as hashing or nearest neighbors, which fail to effectively constrain rapid high-frequency anomalies due to their inability to structure or anomaly-detect specifically. To address this, we introduce ADWIN, a novel, robust technique for anomaly detection on infinite streams that learns optimal retention policies dynamically. Our experimental evaluation, conducted across various real-world streams using both ADWIN and baseline methods (including HW, LRA-ANN, and LRA-Hashing), demonstrates through a novel scoring system that ADWIN significantly surpasses these approaches.

When does judicial knowledge that a respondent possesses a device password allow a court to compel them to unlock the device? Earlier work addressed this problem using the doctrine of *foreseeable conclusion* derived from *Fisher v. US*. This research argues that the threshold for "foreseeable conclusion" can be formulated as a problem involving the graphical visualization of Kayley diagrams, or, as they're known in some circles, Venn diagrams. It sets out an approach to automatically generate such diagrams from literal statements of what the respondent knows. The approach treats each declarative sentence as providing knowledge about the relationship of certainty between the password and some action or inaction by the respondent. By rendering these statements as overlapping regions, the method can generate diagrams that visually represent the inference process and can determine when the information given necessitates that the respondent either do something specific, such as disclosing the password. The authors note further developments, such as considering statements referring to negations or disjunctions. Demonstrations using actual court cases show its capacity to resolve complex, real-world legal scenarios involving layered assertions of knowledge.

Rapidly circulating through social media on a global scale, fake news threatens users and entire communities, especially as it emerges with alarming speed. While deep learning models excel when trained extensively on data for specific events, their effectiveness often declines due to domain shifts when encountering new topics. Consequently, current detection methods face major obstacles when dealing with emergent fake news events, where accumulating large, well-annotated datasets is impractical. Furthermore, integrating knowledge about new events currently necessitates retraining models or continuous fine-tuning—a process that is often costly, inefficient, and unfeasible in real-world applications.

To solve these issues, this paper presents MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework capable of learning to identify fake news from newly emerged events using limited verified data (few-shot setting). The model employs meta-learning techniques to adapt quickly to new events with rapid refinement based on available confirmed data. To enhance adaptation performance, the framework utilizes multiple data augmentation strategies to generate labeled versions of unverified (and inherently fake) samples, enabling robust training on diverse, unlabeled information. Experimental results from TREC's Fake News Challenge demonstrate that MetaFEND effectively detects misinformation on fresh, emerging events in few-shot scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.

Quantum annealing (QA) emerges as a viable strategy for addressing combinatorial optimization problems by embedding their solutions within the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian, employing dual Hamiltonians—one as a driver and one representing the specific problem. If the driver Hamiltonian is switched adiabatically, QA theoretically ensures convergence to this errorless ground state; however, real-world constraints on the speed of this evolution often introduce bit-flips during transitions out of the ground state, typically mitigated through heuristic problem-specific adjustments. When the problem Hamiltonian includes anti-ferromagnetic interactions, it is possible to engineer a scenario where non-trivial quantum effects permanently prevent convergence to the ground state, regardless of annealing duration. This study derives an exact, time-dependent wave-function solution for a spin-1/2 system coupled to a bosonic oscillator, where the coupling is modulated via quantum annealing. We analyze multiple aspects of this dynamic process, specifically examining energy levels and their time evolution, population distributions across different energy manifolds, and the system's entanglement character.

Fiber-reinforced composite materials featuring fillers with tunable electrical conductivity are effective at self-reporting damage. This research examines the extent to which pandemic-related remote learning disrupted or altered the assistance-seeking behaviors of undergraduates. Data was gathered through analysis of open-submission, outsourced tutoring interactions within an online University Physics I course. The study specifically focused on students with prior exposure to in-person instruction but new experiences with remote work, as well as those encountering both instructional formats remotely for the first time. Given that these individuals often constitute a significant and often underrepresented demographic, the primary aim was seeing how pandemic-induced online education impacted their tendency to submit open questions, as well as the complexity and demands of those inquiries. While submission volumes remained statistically consistent across various student demographics during the pandemic, open-question characteristics shifted notably. During the pandemic, submissions demanded less external help and contained more self-generated work, especially among students navigating online learning environments for the first time. This paradox suggests the pandemic did not curb the propensity of first-generation college students to ask questions publicly, though remote learning conditions prompted changes in question framing that could complicate their resolution by tutoring professionals. Such observations highlight essential areas further study, as students from diverse educational backgrounds responded differently to online learning during the pandemic.

While brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) effectively promote upper-body recovery in those suffering from spinal cord trauma, their role in rehabilitative walking support was initially less emphasized, though pioneering noninvasive EEG-based prototypes offered initial feasibility for paraplegic locomotion. To address this, this study deployed high-density electocorticogram (ECoG) signals recorded intracerebrally from two healthy participants walking across treadmill speed ranges. An offline decoding process showed a capacity of distinguishing four distinct walking rates using Empirical Likelihood Functional (ELF) analysis on raw ECoG data, achieving 90% to 100% accuracy via a subject-specific algorithm. Subsequently, subject-specific support vector machine models refined this accuracy at single-rate level 95%. The primary objective involved constructing an implantable BCI system designed for stepwise adjustment of treadmill velocity, yielding 80% user agreement. The findings demonstrate the potential utility of invasive ECoG-decoding methods in regulating mechanical equipment via neural activity.

Various physical setups in condensed matter and atomic fields exhibit a topological transition into new states of matter known as topological insulators. By employing a Fourier transform spectroscopy method, we determine the non-trivial Zak phase of acoustic modes even within strongly localized regimes. Our design includes a time-reversal symmetric mass distribution around a central topological defect in the acoustic Van Der Wauss (VdW) lattice. This configuration yields localized states with a modified Zak phase that persists despite the absence of a bulk band gap, marking the signature of the topological transition in the acoustic Anderson insulating (TAI) system. Furthermore, this effect is demonstrated in multiple modes within the same structure but equipped with different unit cell mass configurations.

To address this, we propose a novel data-driven framework for predicting soil deformation. Dressed masses for both quarks and mesons are established using gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations. While extensive studies exist regarding the nonlinear electrohydrodynamics driving liquid droplet deformation in air, the resulting impact on the adjacent gas remains relatively overlooked. Our observations demonstrate that circulations within air, generated by significant oscillatory deformation of a pendant water droplet suspended within a vibrating electric field, function similarly to micro-scale fans. This aerodynamic effect is evidenced by the rapid expulsion of an air bubble from inside the oscillating droplet, even though internal electrostatic stresses theoretically prohibit immediate penetrations by air or vapor. The generated air currents strongly influence the deposition and removal of airborne particulates, manifesting as distinct temporal oscillations in a droplet's electrostatic charge and its radial growth and to a certain level in electrical discharge lumenarity. However, when exposed to conductive particles, a pendant droplet can experience instantaneous piercing, but only after the surrounding air has been nearly completely deprived of particles and ionized, resulting in a sudden surge in electrical current. This specific phenomenon points to a rapid transition from a dielectrophoretic regime to direct electro-pinning. Such insights provide essential clarity for a deeper comprehension of complex gas–liquid-interactions under intense non-uniform electrical fields and have significant implications for the secure operation of technologies involving airborne ionization, such as those used in aerosol deposition, dielectric barrier discharge plasma sources, and corona-based water purification systems.

Realizing the complete expressive potential of human language is essential for effective human-machine communication, with negation serving as a vital functional component. However, current neural generation models often struggle with the ordered dependency variations and complex patterns inherent in negated transformations, frequently resulting in errors or omission. This study introduces a novel ordered semantic transformation approach to address neural text generation that handles multiple negations. By employingayoilating model to produce transformation trees (TTs) that map source sentences to their negated counterparts and utilizing them as transformation blueprints, our proposed transformation neural generator (TNM) accurately maps negation operators within generated texts. Furthermore, our method correctly implements human instructions specifying negation scopes in the output. Experiments demonstrate that TNMs significantly outperform current state-of-theart models in negation focus generation, correct scope realization, and overall sentence similarity scores containing multi negations, with statistical validity confirmed by STP values.

Information hierarchies typically function as structures to organize and facilitate access to complex data. These systems frequently fail to identify them because they rely on supposing information entities exist in isolation, ignoring inherent relational patterns. This paper presents a methodology for extracting information hierarchies from texts that entities and relations previously extracted via existing techniques. Specifically, the authors characterize simple hierarchies through the lens of maximally coherent subgraph occurrences within description logic-based hierarchical relations. The approach is demonstrated using instance-level headings, a category where all child nodes share a common immediate parent, as introduced by the authors. The method is applied to impose structural order on previously extracted instances of technical document headings, verifying the model with user studies regarding its intended purpose.

Quenching and annealing represent opposing approaches to the time-evolution of quantum systems; annealing slowly adjusts a Hamiltonian's parameters to explore equilibrium phases for solving complex optimizations, while quenching imposes sudden changes that create non-equilibrium states. We examine the connection between both regimes, demonstrating that a dynamical quench parameter—which characterizes the post-quench quantum state—allows us to expose the minimum annealing gap. A key bottleneck for these algorithms, this hidden landscape becomes accessible when combined with statistical methods such as neural network training. These tools reveal how slow annealing dynamics are mirrored within the rapid quench regime, effectively mapping out the underlying gap even if complete knowledge of the annealing Hamiltonian is absent. We specifically highlight the quantum discontinuity factor, a metric of how system distance evolves during gradual annealing, which replaces the traditional geometric definition under quenched conditions. This factor displays distinct singularities signaling the divergences needed to locate the lowest annealing gap. Ultimately, understanding such dynamics enhances our grasp of quantum annealing obstructions and non-equilibrium dynamics, potentially guiding optimizations by illuminating the constraints that limit these solutions.

The phase structure of dense matter within the intermediate density regime—situated between nuclear saturation density and the conditions of the early universe—remains uncertain, as current research relies on various effective field theories whose predictions diverge significantly. In this work, we adopt a pragmatic approach by postulating that sound velocity decreases as density rises with increasing magnitude at high levels, eventually converging to a specific value either by softening or through the emergence of an explicit phase transition defined by either first or second order; associated phase diagrams were consequently generated. Employing the $\gamma$-passage technique, we examined how distinct initial neutron star conditions influence the dynamics and outcomes associated with such transitions in dense conditions. Our findings reveal that varying star conditions yield corresponding differences both in the density thresholds triggering the onset of transitions and in their terminal states occurring at high densities. Furthermore, in scenarios involving sudden heating, it is observed that the density trajectory follows a trajectory at roughly 1.5 to 2 times nuclear saturation density while moving towards the semi-infinite limit; in contrast, progressive heating results in paths traversing densities several times greater before approaching this same limit. Additionally, although timing remains consistent, observable effects such as gravitational wave emissions, elemental compositions, and Grains are noticeably impacted. Finally, it can reasonably be anticipated that under these circumstances, phase transitions will emerge at intermediate intervals, and their resulting density profiles, associated with varying rates, should align differently across scenarios.

We examine a diverse set of non-classical states formed from coherent superpositions of squeezed and displaced number states, analyzing their potential use in high-precision parameter estimation. For each state, we compute the Fisher information associated with an interferometric measurement implemented within an unsensed arm of a Mach–Zehnder interferometer. Present near the beginning of this paper is a detailed investigation into the sensitivity enhancements achievable when these states serve as input. We demonstrate that specific members of this family, characterized by low photon counts, can outperform both classical states and prominent entangled states—such as NOON, coherent, and two-mode squeezed states. Furthermore, these states yield superior performance compared to established quantum-enhanced strategies like phase cancellation, as evidenced when estimating phases via phase-difference methods. Through the concluding section, we investigate how these states behave regarding direct phase estimation in scenarios where photon number counting occurs within both interferometer arms; again, certain members surpass the limits set by classical and bipartite entangled states.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) involves hydrodynamical processes requiring swift gas cooling; it is posited to function in the outer sectors of protoplanetary disks. Although the VSI generates vertical turbulent motions capable of influencing dust accumulation and sinking, dust dynamics can conversely dampen the instability: reduced gas opacity due to dust removal hampers cooling in the already thin outer regions. Utilizing linear analysis, this research quantifies how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. By devising a cooling timescale model that accounts for dust maturation beyond one micron and size-dependent sedimentation, we integrate it with linear stability analysis to determine VSI activity regions (the "VSI zones") and their peak growth rates at various radii. Results indicate that dust maturation and sinking confine the VSI zone more tightly along the midplane, resulting in reduced growth rates due to diminished shear in the vertically weaker velocity fields near the lower disk altitudes. Specifically, for a 0.01 solar mass disk, allowing dust to grow from 10 microns to 1 mm suppresses growth rates by an order of magnitude exceeding 10. Consequently, dust-driven turbulence suppression likely facilitates additional outer-disk dust evolution and accounts for the pronounced settling seen in the HL Tau system.

The rise of outsourcing training and machine learning (ML) model inference has created new attack surfaces, allowing adversaries to embed subtle "backdoors" via data API calls or inference interactions. These backdoors appear harmless normally but activate under specific trigger conditions, forcing erroneous outputs. This study introduces a method to train indistinguishable randomized proxies of black-box models that amplify these backdoors. Although unseen to adversaries, these proxies enable the conduct of intrusive tests for malicious data sources or the deployment of defensive measures on compromised APIs, facilitating the discovery of backdoors even in restricted settings where only input/output access is available. Furthermore, we demonstrate techniques for locating triggers and overwriting the attack with a more potent anomaly within the randomized proxy framework, complementing recent efforts to train such proxies via virtual gradients using backpropagation through stochastic noise. All real-world attack simulations, conducted through actual data APIs or model interfaces, support the claims made through our experimental results.

High-precision astrometry relies on relativistic models of light propagation grounded in the parametrised post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework used to investigate potential general relativistic violations in observational data. Among various PPN parameters, $\gamma$, which quantifies the deflection of light by gravity, significantly influences astrometric measurements. This study analyzes both theoretically and computationally how deviations of PPN $\gamma$ from its General Relativity value of unity impact parallax measurements in Gaia-like missions. By simulating a Gaia-like system with a PPN $\gamma$ deviation of $10^{-3}$, the research identifies an average shift in parallax of approximately $0.45\,\text{mas}$, equivalent to a multiplicative change of around 1 part in 2000. Additionally, the simulations observe increased fluctuations in individual parallax values of nearly $10\,\text{\mu as}$ RMS, arising from the interaction between systematic biases and high-parallax tail distributions. These systematic parallax errors, standing at roughly half a microarcsecond below, introduce a significant hurdle for the ultimate goal of resolving individual exoplanets around stars with parallax magnitudes near $10\,\mu as$. Consequently, this inherent systematic floor necessitates numerical alignment strategies, such as the high-frequency calibration (HFC) method, to achieve full exoplanet detectability.

We offer an accelerated approach for reducing dynamic models to their slowest nonresonant spectral submanifolds using nonlinear data-driven methods. This approach relies on observed data to identify a low-dimensional, attracting stable manifold and then derives a highly sparse representation of the dynamics restricted to this surface. While recent techniques like SSMLearn use implicit optimization for this purpose, the algorithms we introduce reformulate both manifold identification and normal form calculation as direct, explicit problems under specific constraints. Demonstrating significant improvements on both experimental and numerical datasets, these refined algorithms achieve rapid convergence while generating precise, sparse dynamic models.

Standard models yielding 1D or 2D solitons, including Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equations for Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), exhibit Galilean invariance, facilitating the derivation of traveling soliton families from static ones. A significant research goal is identifying models that support stable self-accelerating (SA) soliton solutions. While linear systems possess SA Airy waves, these decay in amplitude. Recently, it was demonstrated that a GP model for two interacting BEC components, which allows for self-interference of the resulting matter wave, predicts various bound soliton structures that remain stable during self-acceleration. However, this paper introduces more generalized 1112 GP systems for coupled BECs. These models are solved using a multi-component Hirota approach, yielding a broad spectrum of 1D soliton solutions. This class encompasses 1D SA solitons stable over time and hybrid states combining SA behavior with rotational or vibrational dynamics. In these latter states, one component shifts position while the other oscillates or rotates around it and remains bound to the first. Utilization of a gauge transformation, these solutions are expressed via arbitrary seed functions. Analysis confirms their stability through numerical simulations and reveals distinct physical properties differing based on whether the components contribute the acceleration individually or collectively.

Utilizing external knowledge to assist machine-based question answering (QA) on tasks requiring commonsense background faces the challenge of overwhelming and misleading information due to the boundless volume of such data. To address this, we introduce a semantics-driven, knowledge-aware QA framework designed to regulate knowledge injection from coarse to fine granularity. We implement a filtering strategy to refine extracted information based on the initial (coarse) semantics of a question and have created a semantics-aware retrieval module. This module leverages structural knowledge inputs and performs hierarchical fusion of appropriate facts aligned with the precise (fine-grained) semantics of questions. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches on the CommonsenseQA benchmark dataset.

Molecular cations appear across diverse astronomical settings, especially in the atmospheres and tails of comets, where sunlight generates intense electromagnetic radiation. Despite their significance, researching these species is challenging due to the complex spectral interference caused by intense neutral molecules. This study introduces the public-release version of 'astroCHAMPS,' a tool designed to compute the electromagnetic spectrum of molecular anions, an crucial component in analyzing and interpreting observed astronomical data. The program utilizes quantum chemistry techniques, specifically relativistic density functional theory, along with various post-Hartree-Fock methods to determine electronic structures, generate spectral simulations, produce output images, and include visualizations of isodensity surfaces for atomic or molecular orbitals. These tools are especially valuable for analyzing complex systems involving extended $\pi$-conjugated structures containing multiple nitrogen atoms. To demonstrate its application, we calculated the spectra of cyano and isocyano coma cations—spectroscopically important but analytically demanding anions found in a cometeous tail. We present a comparative analysis of ground and excited state properties, as well as spectral synthesis, generated using relativistic DFT methods alongside selected post-Hartree-Fock approaches.

There is a long tradition of research, tracing back to Bachet and Lagrange, concerning whether totally positive elements can always be expressed as a sum of squares. For certain specific structures, such as the integers or polynomials with rational coefficients, decomposition methods are well-established; however, the problem remains largely unresolved for many other significant rings and fields. This study introduces an explicit algorithm that expresses elements in any global field (covering both number fields and global function fields) as a sum of squares with minimal length.

We introduce an innovative on-device methodology based on photonics that replaces conventional spectroscopy. This technique performs spectral cross-correlation using a template entirely within the hardware itself, a capability enabled by photonic structures with specifically tailored, modulated transmission spectra. This optical approach eliminates the need for dispersive optics and the slit scanning mechanisms they typically accompany, offering instead the exact speed of light processing speed. We experimentally validate this concept through a prototype optical cross-correlation system built using an Integrated Photonic Circuit (IPC) architecture. The demonstration involves recovering the wavelengths of unknown target signals that share partial spectral overlap with a reference template spectrum embedded within the chip design. The experimental results not only confirm the feasibility of this novel optical computing paradigm but also establish a robust foundation for future applications in spectrum analysis and retrieval.

This work addresses the challenge of maintaining a global machine learning model across a distributed set of communication-constrained nodes with heterogeneous capacities, where practical implementations are further complicated by asymmetric data availability and limited online training feasibility due to privacy concerns. While standard approaches either assume ideal data centralization or rely on a virtual participant that assumes equal weighted contributions based on a naive population estimate, these methods often fail in reality. Key contributions include a novel definition of skew relevant to online FL, the development of adaptive methods tailored for environments with budget and capacity restrictions, and analytical insights into convergence rates, outlier influence, and comparative performance against standard algorithms.

Although rotating turbulence is typically associated with inverse cascades dominated by rotationally symmetric, geostrophic vortices, it is increasingly recognized that it can also support fully three-dimensional states exhibiting a downscale energy transfer. This study applies direct numerical simulations within a multiply periodic domain where geostrophic motions are deliberately dissipationed to explore the statistical characteristics of three-dimensional rotating turbulence. The generated flow behaves as inertial wave turbulence and strictly adheres to the analytically predicted Zakharov-Kolgrov spectral model by Galtier, thereby substantiating numerical evidence for the significance of wave turbulence theory applied to 3D, direction-dependent wave systems. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that applying identical forcing conditions can yield either wave or geostrophic turbulence based on initial state inputs, providing additional support for the existence of bi-stability in such flows. This letter contributes further evidence.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. Drawing upon data from North Carolina courts covering 1994 to 2009, this study analyzes whether requiring offenders on probation to receive mental healthcare lowers their subsequent likelihood of reincarceration. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis contrasts individuals mandated to participate in treatment programs with those under probation without such requirements. The findings reveal that mandating treatment reduces recidivism within three years by a margin of 5.6 percentage points—or 17 percent—compared to non-treatment probationers. While specific impacts on violent and property crimes demonstrate reduced recurrence, the beneficial trends also intensify as time progresses post-conviction. Finally, a cost-benefit assessment indicates that resulting decreases in crime sufficiently reimburse expenses associated with offering these programs.

Deferred Neural Rendering achieves a distinguished compromise between computational demands and visual fidelity by combining traditional rendering with neural methods. Extending this DNR framework to handle articulated bodies via skinned meshes promises diverse new capabilities. However, introducing unbounded objects and varying light geometry into a system designed for bounded, fixed scenes requires significant developments. To address these challenges within DNR presents an opportunity to accelerate real-time generation of high-quality virtual human models. Our solution adapts DNR's view and appearance decomposition and employs an enhanced set of metrics to render dynamic bodies, using orthographic projection and infinite material definitions. We also derive new viewing terms and sum them into a consistent viewing geometry to manage deformed vertex positions. This approach allows us to invert the appearance equation and recover appearance residuals, which we utilize for texture recovery and ABR rendering targets. To streamline this process, we apply the Jacobi inverse of the binding matrix as an approximation for shape key interpolation, significantly reducing rendering requirements compared to conventional methods. Our method requires only a single input image, leveraging implicit generalization across binding axes to produce realistic human models without the demand for extensive retargeting datasets often required by Telemav et al's method. In addition, our framework supports multiple views and enhances visual quality through an improved lighting representation. As the foundation, Deferred Neural Rendering remains applicable, with our approach integrating seamlessly. Comparisons show that our technique surpasses SOTA results. Measuring atomic disorder levels is vital for understanding how changes in local structural environments influence material performance and longevity. This study utilizes graph neural networks to establish a physically interpretable index for local disorder. This index characterizes the variety of immediate atomic arrangements as a smooth continuum ranging from solid to liquid states, evaluated relative to thermal fluctuations. We demonstrate this new approach across three representative cases with distinct disorder levels: solid-liquid interfaces, polycrystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries. Focusing specifically on aluminum, we illustrate how this method captures the spatiotemporal development of such boundaries, including a rigorous mathematical definition of the boundary separating order and disorder within space. Additionally, we identify physics-consistent gradients emerging from these continuous disorder maps to aid in evaluating and forecasting material behavior and potential failures. Collectively, our framework offers a conceptual and adaptable method for linking complicated local atomic architectures to broader material phenomena.

Given a parametric family $f(y|\theta)$ for $\theta \in \Omega$, let $\eta(\theta)$ represent a specific function and $G$ be an unknown mixing distribution. The objective is to estimate the expected value $E_G(\eta(\theta)) \equiv \eta_G$ using a set of independent observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$. Here, the data samples are $i.d.d$. drawn such that $Y_i \sim f(y|\theta_i)$ and parameters $\theta_i \sim G$ are also independent and identified identically. The paper investigates Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLEs) within this framework. Key properties of these estimators are established, including their consistency, asymptotic normality, and convergence in distribution of the associated mixing distribution. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of $\eta_{\hat{G}_n}$—where $\hat{G}_n$ is the GMLE for $G$—is detailed when $\eta_\cdot$ maps $\Omega$ to either $\mathbb{R}$ or the cone of nonnegative definite matrices. Finally, the theoretical findings are demonstrated through two concrete applications: the compound Poisson process and the Skew-Normal distribution.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) applies students' historical interaction records to model their evolving knowledge states and predict their future learning outcomes. While deep learning-based approaches for KT have recently achieved significant advancements, the exact drivers behind these DL-KT models remain elusive, and their proper evaluation and analysis continue to be difficult tasks. Specifically, existing methods typically rely on proprietary and custom data cleaning workflows, impeding experimental standardization. Moreover, these studies often utilize varying metrics that obscure cross-model comparisons. To resolve these issues, we present *n-KT*, a unified, configurable neural framework designed to lower the absolute and relative operational thresholds for DL-KT research. By implementing rigorous experiments across two extensive datasets using this model, we establish normalized evaluation protocols, uncover effective data cleanings strategies, reveal underlying learning mechanisms, identify influential data factors, assess the impact of various components, and verify robust performance. In summary, we introduce *n-KT* not merely as a baseline for future DL-KT investigations but as a mandatory tool for proper, systematic knowledge tracing.

This work demonstrates that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses a closed range within the smooth function space $C^\infty(M)$ on any manifold $M$. Moreover, for any manifold $M$ lacking compact subcomponents, the operator $P$ demonstrates surjectivity on $C^\infty(M)$, with applications yielding to Helmholtz theory explored accordingly.

The version of the proof format adopted by the veriT SMT solver was initially showcased ten years ago following the first PxTP workshop. Since its inception, this format has fully evolved to the point where it supports various SMT applications, with other proof-producing solvers also generating files in this format. To secure a better direction for future advancements in this format, this article aims to solicit input from practitioners. To achieve that, it will examine the evolution history of the format as well as the strategies used for its maintenance until now.

Synchronous updates in cross-device federated learning often require a pre-defined quota of active clients per communication round, yet the required number increases costably, creating challenges when the total available clients is finite. When the total number of enrolled clients is finite and the number of active participants per round is unbounded, the number of active clients can grow without limit as rounds progress; however, this sparseness introduces challenges in maintaining the number of active clients in later iterations. To circumvent this issue without imposing a quota on active participants, we propose modifying the client selection probability via a weighted stochastic sampling approach applied to the non-uniform weights under the condition that client selection probability must adjust. The convergence analysis of our approach demonstrates parameter consistency, yet may not achieve optimal rates. Nevertheless, empirical evaluations reveal significant efficiency gains over existing methodologies, even if we do not guarantee the fastest theoretical convergence. If the number of participants per round is unbounded and selection probability adjustment is implemented, our method proves effective in enhancing performance, yet may still require comparison with theoretically optimal benchmarks for maximum potential.

Recent advancements in Character-level Joint Training (C-Joint) for automatic speech recognition achieve a lower average word error rate than using the full alphabet, likely due to enhanced generalization through varied writing scenarios and the smooth variation of language across diverse scripts. Our investigation explores using intermediate alphabets in C-Joint training. Our method creates these lists by adding more weights to specific letters in converted script based on their position within the word, forming an expanded intermediate alphabet. We validate this approach on the Common Voice dataset with Hebrew audio samples, finding that models trained via our intermediate alphabet outperform those using both standard Hebrew character sets (via C-Joint) and English-transcribed Hebrew by roughly 4–5 percentage points in Word Accuracy Rate. These results indicate that automatic speech models processed through an intermediate alphabet find it helpful in learning from multi-linguistic data via translated scripts.

Proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embeddings serve as a crucial technique in mining and learning within knowledge graphs. This research introduces a novel, efficient approach dedicated to extracting embeddings from the Wikipedia graph by leveraging node features and relationships derived from knowledge bases, alongside methods for assessing their quality. Our study reveals that the integrated use of these methods results in high-quality Node Representations that effectively capture both local neighborhood context and global informational structures within the graph. Furthermore, downstream applications demonstrate that this framework confers substantial advantages in emerging graph-based tasks, including citation formatting, entity linking, and knowledge graph prediction.

We propose that the enigma surrounding the $f_X(1500)$ state, first noted over a decade ago by us and recently addressed by LHCb in the $K\bar{K}\gamma$ final state, can be resolved by identifying it as a hidden scalar flactator, $Sc_1$. Motivated existing data from BaBar, CLEO, and Delphi, along with our own recent analysis, we present a coherent theoretical framework that reinterpretes existing $f_0$ meson measurements as consistent identifiers for $Sc_1$. Furthermore, we suggest that the puzzering $B^0\bar{K}^0$ oscillations reported by Delige are actually signature of $B^0\bar{K}^0$ oscillations that proceed via the intermediate decay channel $B^0\to f_X(1500)\bar{K}^0\gamma$, with $f_X(1500)\bar{K}^0\gamma\to f_0\bar{K}^0\gamma$. In light of these ideas future studies of $B^0\bar{K}^0$ oscillations in the $B^0\to f_X(1500)\bar{K}^0\gamma final state represent a key step toward ultimately settling the matter.

The study presents a highly effective force transmission approach for series elastic actuators (SEAs) centered on a Transmission Force Observer (TFOB) for estimating force. This methodology addresses force detection challenges in SEAs, specifically mitigations caused by nonlinear variations within elastic transmissions, sensor noise, and measurement discrepancies in deformation sensing components. Initially, research explores inherent limitations in current SEA transmission force detection methods to establish a strong basis—through the examination of stochastic attributes—for achieving precise performance when the observer-based approach is utilized as a primary solution. The proposed TFOB is derived through analysis of a heightened mathematical model representing deformation behavior in these elastic systems, serving as an enhancement to standard techniques for detecting force transmission issues. Furthermore, a quantitative framework is established to evaluate force estimation accuracy attributed directly to these complex, nonlinear deformation characteristics. Experimental validation is provided using an SEA physical prototype to confirm the practical viability and efficacy of this proposed transmission strategy.

A particle raft suspended on an elongating liquid substrate serves as a large-scale analog for material rupture. The temporal resolution of this setup permits the observation of both particle relaxation and the development of cracks. Experiments show that the raft undergoes uniaxial stretching as the air-fluid interface beneath it expands, resulting in morphologies that shift continuously with stretching speed. These patterns arise from a balance between two mechanisms: the speed of re-aggregation—where viscous and capillary forces drive particles toward a low-energy state—and the velocity differential between adjacent particles induced by flow expansion. The interaction between the characteristic timescales of expansion and relaxation dictates whether rafts develop into the specific morphologies described here. The time to relaxation decreases rapidly with increasing particle size and size, while expansion can be manipulated via particle shape and stretching velocity to produce or prevent failure. Theoretical models align well with these observations, offering predictive understanding of the raft dynamics under such stress.

We examine SU(Nc) gauge theories in three dimensions incorporating degenerate complex scalar multicomponent fields (where Nf exceeds 1) that belong to the fundamental representation, respecting both global U(Nf) symmetry and SU(Nc) gauge symmetry, and subject to the general J=0 quartic potential. Our investigation determines conditions under which this potential yields zero vacuum energy while preventing charge-type and Q-ball instabilities for fields of any Nf value (with Nf=2 and Nf=3 examples demonstrating these conditions are met). Moreover, we demonstrate that the J=0 potential drives first-order phase transitions between phase transitions characterized by spontaneous symmetry determination and those involving gauge field condensation, with the latter occurring due to a "fourth order" mechanism analogous to the XY model, particularly for larger Nf counts. This result aligns with findings from pure three-dimensional SU(Nc) gauge theories regarding the analogy to four-dimensional Witten's reasoning regarding phase transitions in SU(Nc) gauge group variants.

This paper examines sorting networks built from comparators that take $k$ inputs and max out two specified vectors component-wise. When $k=2$, these are known as comparators. We denote by $S_n(k)$ the minimal depth achievable for sorting $n$ inputs via such networks. It is trivially clear that $S_n(k)$ grows linearly with $n$: $S_n(k)=O(n)$ with constant dependence. Previously established findings confirmed this bound for $k=2$ (Bender and Ahi, SODA 2008) and extended it to fixed depths where $k=\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ (Berenstein al., SODA. 2012). We enhance the result, demonstrating this linear lower limit extends even deeper, so that for any fixed depth, $k=\Theta(n^{1/D})$. Additionally, leveraging this result on sorting networks, we have created random sorting networks (k=2) of fixed depth $D=\Theta(d)$, which satisfy central limit behavior under Barenstein et al's notation for $k=\sqrt{n}$, or more accurately, when generalized, for input size k=2, it is known to be $\theta(d)$. Finally noted is how this satisfies Barenstein et al's condition, showing convergence to normal distribution instead under generalized parameters where $k=\theta(d^{-})$.
