This paper details our submission for the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Challenge, which focuses on classifying Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical conditions based on chest CT images for COVID-19 cases. Our methodology utilizes a newly developed Infection-Aware 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network tailored for severity grading. Specifically, we deploy two sequential segmentation models to isolate the lung region and subsequently the internal infected areas; this derived segmentation mask is then used to enhance the original CT slices with complementary data. Addressing imbalanced data distribution, we optimize an advanced Contrastive Mixup architecture through weighted cross-entropy loss. Consequently, our method achieved first place on the challenge's test set, establishing a new state-of-the-art score of 0.814 for the Macro F1 metric.

While most current Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) techniques primarily concentrate on generating extensive pseudo-training data to improve performance, very few tackle the challenge of few-shot domain adaptation. This study redefines various GEC environments as distinct tasks and introduces a novel approach called FUSENO, which integrates unsupervised domain adaptation and meta-learning to achieve high accuracy in low-data scenarios without relying on parallel corpora for the target domains. In FUSENO, the back-bone neural network is constructed via the combination of multiple components, with specific domains adapting by selectively activating certain modules. The selection mechanism and the parameterization of adaptive weights are optimized through meta-learning. Experimental results across varying levels of domain granularity indicate that FUSENO significantly surpasses strong baselines, especially when applied to single-domain settings. Additionally, the approach achieves superior performance in challenging settings involving finer-grained tasks given very limited training samples ($N=1$).

In practice, numerical rounding is ubiquitous. While research has historically addressed the impact of rounding on continuous random variables, this practice necessitates a study of its effects on discrete distributions as well. This paper introduces the estimation and inference methods for a non-negative discrete random variable $X$ subject to arithmetic rounding. In this framework, an observed value $Y$ either equals $X$ or represents the rounded result of $X$. The mapping determined by the rounding method partitions the non-negative integers into intervals, with $Y$ providing information regarding which interval contains the true value of $X$. We develop a general likelihood function for this scenario and derive its properties for specific rounding schemes, including "round half up" and "round to even." Furthermore, these techniques are extended to handle cases where the support of $X$ is limited to a known interval. Statistical inference elements such as parameter estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing are also established. Finally, we demonstrate these approaches through simulation studies and analyze real-world datasets.

We examined the crystal structure and magnetic behavior of single crystalline hexagonal lanthanum-free rare-earth indium oxides (specifically $\text{GdInO}_3$) by integrating experimental data with modeling. This material contains a honeycomb lattice of indium atoms arranged in bilayers, separated by gadolinium (Gd) monolayers; neutron scattering results confirm that Gd indium layers exhibit A-type antiferromagnetic ordering, characterized by ferromagnetic alignment within layers and antiferromagnetic alternation between adjacent layers along the $c$-axis. This magnetic arrangement arises from competing exchange interactions, primarily driven by the strong indium–indron (RI) coupling, which stabilizes the R layers into self-composed pairs with a magnetic ordering transition temperature ($T_{\text{n}}$) of 23.6 K. Furthermore, Gd layers adjacent to these In-Gd monolayer groups transition antiferromagnetically to the direction of the crystal $b$-axis, marked with a transition temperature ($T_2$) of 14.2 K, behavior attributed to the dominant van Vleck indium dipolar interaction. The study concludes that competing exchange forces between the Gd and In magnetic moments, combined with direction-specific magnetic anisotropy, are responsible for establishing the observed $O$-type (or A-type) magnetic order in this specific structure of $\text{GdInO}_

This paper examines the allocation of indivisible goods among strategic agents with additive valuation functions, operating in a non-monetary setting where a mechanism is allocated based on a reported preference profile. The study investigates the existence of undominated strategies within the mechanism and applies evolutionary game theory via the replicator dynamic to explore long-term behavioral convergence. Specifically, we analyze pure strategy profiles that are robust to evolutionary invasion by other strategies introduced in small numbers. We demonstrate that for any monotone resource allocation mechanism, any profile satisfying envy-freeness up to one item (EF1)—where no agent prefers another's bundle more than their own after removing some good—is resistive to evolutionary disruption; moreover, under specific conditions, such profiles support undominated strategies. These contributions broaden previous research by addressing a broader spectrum of mechanisms and equilibrium concepts while formulating a costly communication game where truthful revelation is proven to be undominant along the evolutionary path. In a related scenario involving a costly communication framework, truthful reporting emerges as a dominant strategy within its cost functions.

This work examines the unstopped English-to-French domain adaptation task. Since collecting aligned bilingual datasets for test scenarios is impractical, we assume access to a test-only dataset in English only. To improve features from source data that contains label annotations, we aim to generate test labels using machine translation in the source space. We specifically explore the utilization of translators across two methods: translating directly within the target feature space and introducing translation variability at the feature source. We contrast these approaches, finding that incorporating stochastic translation in the target feature space yields improved performance on these benchmarks. We also provide evidence that this outcome is primarily attributed to the difficulty of mapping data to the target feature system rather than labeling the test dataset. Translating cross-feature systems thus presents a beneficial strategy for such tasks.

The low surface brightness (LSB) spiral UGC 8839 rarely exhibits stellar formation, with a notable exception being a massive HII region complex situated at its outermost disc edge. To investigate the origins and characteristics of this cluster, researchers compared new Hα images alongside archival photometric images of UGC 8839 against similar data for four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings indicate that the off-center star formation in UGC 8839 arises from a hyper-stable, dark matter-dominated disc where the HII region complex stands alone. In contrast, for all observationally studied galaxies, such complexes break down into sub-clusters. UGC 8839 is distinguished by its significantly brighter central bulge and strong, large-scale magnetic fields, particularly within the HII region's domain. While the magnitude and extended scale of the formation complex suggest driver mechanisms such as superwinds and magnetically-supported superbubbles, the article concludes that a heavy ionized radiation field likely constitutes the dominant driver. The article posits that the combination of the local radiation field and magnetic fields creates the observed hyper-stable, long-lived complex.

Paleo-detectors represent a proposed experimental method for searching for dark matter that diverges from the conventional use of tonne-scale instruments monitoring for years or decades. Instead, paleo-detectors analyze small samples of ultra-pure, radiation-hardened scintillator material from the early universe—their namesake origin of the term "paleo". These ancient samples could potentially detect WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles) or other dark matter theories that were too insensitive to conventional methods due to current experimental limits or the need for longer observation times. Because paleo-detectors rely on small masses to achieve maximum sensitivity over long times, extending their capability into the "ultra-weak force regime" where standard tests fail. Even with reduced sample mass, extending the duration of data collection to look back into the deep past allows these detectors access to stronger interaction rates from when the Sun system was younger and densest, potentially covering new uncharted territory for weakly interacting massive particle searches. This approach preserves the historical context by utilizing cosmological timescales, effectively trading observational duration for both higher statistical significance in detecting rare events and the ability to probe extremely low recoil energies characteristic of very weak forces between particles. By utilizing deep-time sampling, researchers retain the potential for detecting dark matter across multiple orders of magnitude below current capabilities, particularly for ultra-weak forces not accessible today.

This study presents the concept of update pattern leakage as a novel risk in modern encrypted databases. It formalizes the definition and security model of DP-Sync specifically regarding data processing (DP) update patterns, while outlining a corresponding DP-Sync framework that upgrades current encrypted database systems to support DP-Sync through DP-compatible updates. The proposed protocol ensures strong protection for the full data evolution history on the stored structures by applying differential privacy principles governing how data owners perform their local data sync operations.

Given the widespread use of Deep Learning in security-critical areas, the importance of understanding model decisions for ensuring appropriate behavior cannot be overlooked, which drives the need for models that are explainable. However, most existing evaluation methods rely on known input labels, a setup where even inaccurate models appear statistically significant due to large data volumes, thereby promoting adoption in critical domains despite risks. This paper introduces a probabilistic framework for assessing explainability that addresses this by treating input labels as unknown. We demonstrate the application of this methodology through a detailed case study on detecting Chat-based sexual predators, showing how it identifies and addresses the inherent biases in traditional metrics, and serving as a bridge to further research.

Minimally invasive surgeries allow for internal abdominal organ examination and have become increasingly favored over open procedures because of their high efficacy. Advancements in hardware, such as high-definition cameras, and software, including artificial intelligence and advanced image processing, have significantly enhanced the visualization of these internal organs during surgery. Since the success of minimally invasive procedures heavily relies on 2D video image quality—specifically achieving a 3D mental image from two views—we developed an all-3D endoscopic framework utilizing vision-language models grounded in single-view 3D reconstruction. This new system enables surgical scene interpretation via dual 3D volumetric representations and facilitates navigation by leveraging stereo endoscopic image pairs to generate precise organ segmentation. Our method first renders virtual light fields from a single viewpoint based on one 2D endoscopic image to support the generation of 3D volumetric images, which in turn aids in distinguishing between different tissues. Subsequently, we utilize parallax from consecutive stereo endoscopic images to drive interactive navigation and locate specific organs. Experimental results across multiple surgeries demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach; furthermore, qualitative ablation studies qualify the key factors contributing to its success.

Current public person Re-Identification (ReID) datasets remain too small by modern standards due to the challenges of labeling, despite the availability of vast amounts of unlabeled surveillance footage which are relatively inexpensive to acquire. A significant problem is harnessing these videos to learn robust ReID representations; notably, most existing methods for unsupervised and domain-agnostic ReID rely on these small public sets stripped of labels, often requiring fine-tuning on unlabeled test domain data to perform well. Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in large-scale contrastive self-supervised image classification, this work proposes generating ReID representations solely from extensive unlabeled surveillance video. By integrating off-the-shelf pedestrian detectors, contrastive losses are applied effectively across both image-level and tracklet-level data. Complementing this approach, principal component analysis utilizes freely accessible camera labels, and evaluation results derived from a large-scale unlabeled benchmark demonstrate performance that far exceeds current state-of-the-art methods.

This research introduces a novel measurement equation for threshold selection within Realized-GARCH models. The developed framework integrates a nonlinear threshold regression scheme to capture the leverage effect and represent the simultaneous linkage between observed realized metrics and latent volatility. Estimation of the model utilizes Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, with its credibility tested through simulations. Further validation involving the application of the suggested measurement equation within Realized-GARCH variants is conducted via an empirical analysis, specifically forecasting the 1% Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for six stock indices using two varying out-of-sample durations. The study demonstrates that the proposed methodology generates comparable tail risk forecasts when benchmarked against traditional GARCH and Realized-GARCH models.
